The marriage rite includes several significant elements: Panigrahana (taking the bride's hand), circumambulation of the fire, Saptapadi (seven steps taken together), and the viewing of the pole star and the star Arundhati, among others — the Rigveda's Surya-sukta (Mandala 10, Sukta 84 [as printed]) supplies the mantras specifically used in marriage. Panigrahana signifies that the couple are no longer to be separated. Having the bride step on a stone (Ashmarohana) signifies she should remain as steadfast as that stone. The Saptapadi — seven steps taken together — signifies that from that point on, the couple will share equally in life's joys and sorrows. The Lajahoma is the bride's fire-offering of puffed rice. Provision for a widow's remarriage is indicated where circumstances allow. In the Dhruva-darshana, the couple view the fire and then the pole star; in the Arundhati-darshana, the bride views and venerates the star Arundhati — signifying that, following the example of the sage Vasishtha's devoted wife Arundhati, she should conduct herself as a virtuous wife who raises worthy children and manages the household well. Since these marriage customs have changed little since Vedic times, much the same practices continue even today.
